scenes.text: You apply for a job, and get a rejection email within minutes. [1] Did a human even read your CV? Often, software screened it first. [2] Let's break down how resume screening, or ATS, works.

Here's the flow. [1] You upload your CV. [2] The system parses it, pulling out your name, skills, jobs, and education. [3] It compares them to the job description. [4] It gives each candidate a match score, [5] and recruiters see a ranked shortlist.

[1] ATS stands for applicant tracking system. [2] It's software companies use to collect and organise job applications. [3] Older systems matched exact keywords. [4] Newer ones use AI and embeddings, to match meaning, so machine learning can match M L.

data.definition: Applicant Tracking System: software that collects, parses and ranks job applications for recruiters.

scenes.text: There are two ways to match. [1] Keyword matching looks for exact words from the job post. It misses synonyms. [2] Semantic matching, using embeddings, understands that people describe the same skill in different ways.

So how do you get through? [1] Use a simple layout. Fancy tables and images can confuse the parser. [2] Mirror important skills from the job description, honestly. [3] And show results with numbers, like, cut costs by 20 percent.
Here's a common myth. [1] People think hiding keywords in white text will trick the system. [2] Modern systems and recruiters can spot this, and it can get you rejected. Honest, clear CVs work best.

data.myth: Hiding keywords in white text tricks the system.
data.fact: Modern systems and recruiters spot it, and it can get you rejected.

scenes.text: Remember bias from episode 42? [1] One famous hiring tool learned to downgrade CVs mentioning women's activities, because of past data. [2] So good companies now run bias audits, [3] and keep humans making the final decisions.
